The Boodie (Bettongia lesueur) is a small, potoroid marsupial endemic to Australian arid and semi-arid zones, where it inhabits dense spinifex hummocks and burrows. Under controlled captive conditions maintaining a stable core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], gestation is remarkably brief at 21 days [tg = 21 days], a developmental interval that reflects the marsupial strategy of giving birth to altricial, underdeveloped young that complete much of their growth while attached to a teat in the maternal pouch. The female produces three litters per year [F_R_i = three litters per year], each consisting of a single pup [N_R_i = each consisting of a single pup], a combination that yields a modest maximum reproductive rate. The neonatal mass at parturition is just 0.317 grams [Wwb = 0.317 grams], a value characteristic of the extremely precocial but diminutive newborns typical of the Macropodiformes, which weigh orders of magnitude less than their mother's adult mass. This tiny joey crawls unaided from the birth canal to the pouch, where it attaches permanently to a teat for an extended nursing phase.

The nursing period in the Boodie is prolonged, reflecting the slow developmental pace typical of many small marsupials. At the stable thermal conditions within the maternal pouch, approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the time since birth at weaning is 165 days [tx = 165 days], at which point the juvenile attains a wet weight of 300 grams [Wwx = 300 grams] and begins to consume solid food while still occasionally suckling. This weaning mass represents a substantial increase from the neonatal weight, though it is still only a fraction of the adult body size. The dependence on milk for such an extended period imposes considerable energetic demands on the female, who must maintain sufficient foraging success to sustain her own metabolism while provisioning a growing joey. After nutritional independence, the young Boodie enters a protracted juvenile phase during which it continues to refine its foraging skills and establish a home range before reaching reproductive competence.

Sexual maturation in Bettongia lesueur occurs well after weaning, marking a gradual transition to the reproductively active adult state. Under the thermally neutral conditions experienced by this species at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 218 days [tp = 218 days], meaning that individuals become capable of reproduction approximately seven months after parturition. This pubertal age is relatively delayed for a mammal of its body size, but aligns with the potoroid pattern of investing in a sustained growing period before the first oestrus. Following the attainment of sexual maturity, a female may enter oestrus and, if successfully mated, begin the cycle again with the short gestation characteristic of the species. The onset of reproductive activity thus represents a key life-history milestone that couples somatic growth with the initiation of costly breeding effort.

Adult Boodies reach a maximum wet body weight of 1300 grams [Wwi = 1300 grams], a modest size compared to many macropodids but typical for a burrow-dwelling potoroid that relies on digging for fungal sporocarps, tubers, and invertebrate prey. This asymptotic mass is attained gradually after puberty, with growth rates slowing as individuals approach their final structural size. The longevity of this species has been recorded in captivity, where individuals maintained at a thermoneutral temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] have a maximum lifespan of approximately 9.9 years [am = approximately 9.9 years], an impressive duration for a small marsupial and one that suggests a slow life-history pace with low extrinsic mortality in its natural habitat when protected from introduced predators. This extended lifespan allows multiple reproductive opportunities across several breeding seasons, facilitating population persistence despite the small litter size.

Comparative analyses with related potoroids and bettongs reveal that the Boodie’s life-history strategy is characterized by a combination of low fecundity, extended developmental phases, and remarkable longevity. The weaning period and interval to puberty in this species are both longer than those reported for the more fecund, short-lived potoroids, consistent with a slower-paced life history that buffers environmental unpredictability. The extremely low neonatal mass, just 0.317 grams [Wwb = 0.317 grams] at birth, underscores the extreme altriciality of marsupial reproduction, while the 21-day gestation (21 days) [tg = 21 days] ranks among the shortest known for any mammal, highlighting the trade-off between rapid parturition and prolonged postnatal development at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The maximum reproductive rate of 3 pups per year [Ri = 3 pups per year] means that at the stable 36 °C [T = 36 °C] conditions typical of captive environments, females produce three litters annually, each with a single pup, a strategy that can sustain populations under favorable rainfall-driven food availability.
